title: The error correction model: short run, long run, speed of adjustment

explain.prompt: Interpret the WTI ~ Brent ECM in 5–7 sentences: what do β (long run), γ (short run) and α (adjustment) mean, with numbers and units? Translate α into a half-life. Why must α be negative? And why is the coffee ~ Brent ECM, with its half-life of 118 days, meaningless?
rubric: β ≈ 0.98 (long run): in equilibrium a 1 % higher Brent goes with ≈ 0.98 % higher WTI; the error-correction term is today's deviation from that relation (≈ the WTI discount vs its normal level).
γ ≈ 0.89 (short run): on the day Brent moves 1 %, WTI moves ≈ 0.89 % — the rest of the adjustment comes later through the error correction.
α ≈ −0.115 (t ≈ −7.7): each day, about 11.5 % of yesterday's deviation is closed; half-life = ln(0.5)/ln(1 + α) ≈ 5.7 business days.
α must be negative for the deviation to shrink: if WTI is too expensive relative to Brent (positive deviation), its next move is pushed down. α ≥ 0 would mean no return to equilibrium.
The ECM is only meaningful if the series are cointegrated: coffee–Brent is not (EG p ≈ 0.50), so its α (−0.006, t ≈ −1.6) and half-life describe nothing real.
The ECM combines both pieces of information that a model in differences alone would discard: short-run co-movement and long-run equilibrium.
